1 Chronicles.author: Anonymous; traditionally associated with Ezra, though the book itself does not name an author.
1 Chronicles.purpose: To retell Israel's history with special emphasis on David, temple worship, priesthood, and continuity with God's covenant promises.
1 Chronicles.theme: God's people find identity and hope through covenant continuity, faithful worship, and the Davidic promise.
1 Chronicles.summary: After extensive genealogies, 1 Chronicles focuses on David's reign, especially his preparation for the temple and organization of worship.

movements.title: Genealogies and Israel's Identity
movements.description: Long genealogies connect the post-exilic community with Israel's ancestral story.

movements.title: David's Reign
movements.description: David unites Israel, brings the ark to Jerusalem, and receives covenant promises.

movements.title: Preparation for the Temple
movements.description: David gathers materials and organizes Levites, priests, musicians, and leaders for future temple worship.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.description: The central figure, presented as Israel's model king who organizes worship and prepares for the temple.

keyFigures.name: Saul
keyFigures.description: Israel's first king, whose death in battle opens the way for David's reign.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.description: David's son, chosen by God to build the temple.

keyFigures.name: Nathan
keyFigures.description: The prophet who delivers God's covenant promise to David.

keyFigures.name: Jabez
keyFigures.description: A man named in the genealogies who prays for God's blessing and protection.

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.description: A Levite appointed by David to lead music and praise before the ark.

keyFigures.name: Ornan the Jebusite
keyFigures.description: Owner of the threshing floor that David purchases, which becomes the site of the temple.

2 Chronicles.author: Anonymous; traditionally associated with Ezra.
2 Chronicles.purpose: To retell the history of Judah with emphasis on temple worship, reform, repentance, and the consequences of covenant faithfulness or rebellion.
2 Chronicles.theme: Seeking God brings renewal, while persistent unfaithfulness brings judgment; restoration remains possible through repentance.
2 Chronicles.summary: 2 Chronicles begins with Solomon's temple, follows Judah's kings with special attention to reforms, and ends with exile and Cyrus's decree permitting return.

movements.title: Solomon Builds the Temple
movements.description: The temple is constructed, dedicated, and filled with God's glory.

movements.title: Reform and Apostasy among Judah's Kings
movements.description: Kings such as Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah pursue reforms, while others lead Judah into sin.

movements.title: Exile and Cyrus's Decree
movements.description: Jerusalem falls to Babylon, but the book ends with permission for the exiles to return and rebuild.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.description: Builds and dedicates the temple, which God's glory fills.

keyFigures.name: The Queen of Sheba
keyFigures.description: Visits Solomon and marvels at his wisdom.

keyFigures.name: Rehoboam
keyFigures.description: Solomon's son, during whose reign the kingdom divides.

keyFigures.name: Asa
keyFigures.description: A king of Judah who leads early reforms but later relies on foreign alliances.

keyFigures.name: Jehoshaphat
keyFigures.description: A king who sends teachers of the law and trusts God in battle.

keyFigures.name: Joash
keyFigures.description: Crowned as a child after Athaliah's usurpation; restores the temple but later turns away.

keyFigures.name: Uzziah
keyFigures.description: A strong king struck with a skin disease after pridefully burning incense in the temple.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.description: A king who reopens the temple, celebrates Passover, and trusts God against Assyria.

keyFigures.name: Manasseh
keyFigures.description: An idolatrous king who, uniquely in Chronicles, repents while in captivity.

keyFigures.name: Josiah
keyFigures.description: The last great reforming king, who renews the covenant and celebrates a great Passover.

keyFigures.name: Cyrus
keyFigures.description: King of Persia whose decree permits the exiles to return.

Ezra.author: Traditionally associated with Ezra; likely uses memoirs, lists, letters, and other records.
Ezra.audience: The returned Jewish community in Judah.
Ezra.purpose: To recount the return from exile, rebuilding of the temple, and Ezra's efforts to restore covenant faithfulness.
Ezra.theme: God restores His people, and restoration includes both rebuilt worship and renewed obedience.
Ezra.summary: Ezra recounts two major returns from exile: one connected with Zerubbabel and the temple, and a later one led by Ezra to address covenant faithfulness.

movements.title: Return and Altar Rebuilt
movements.description: A group returns under Persian authorization and restores sacrificial worship.

movements.title: Temple Rebuilt
movements.description: After opposition and delay, the second temple is completed.

movements.title: Ezra's Reform
movements.description: Ezra arrives with another group and addresses serious covenant concerns within the community.

keyFigures.name: Cyrus
keyFigures.description: King of Persia who issues the decree allowing the exiles to return and rebuild the temple.

keyFigures.name: Zerubbabel
keyFigures.description: A descendant of David who leads the first return and the rebuilding of the temple.

keyFigures.name: Jeshua
keyFigures.description: The high priest who works with Zerubbabel to restore the altar and temple.

keyFigures.name: Haggai and Zechariah
keyFigures.description: Prophets who encourage the people to resume temple construction.

keyFigures.name: Darius
keyFigures.description: Persian king who confirms Cyrus' decree and supports the completion of the temple.

keyFigures.name: Artaxerxes
keyFigures.description: Persian king who commissions Ezra to lead a later group and teach the law.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.description: A priest and scribe skilled in the law of Moses, who leads reforms in Jerusalem.

Nehemiah.author: Largely based on Nehemiah's memoirs, with editorial shaping in its final form.
Nehemiah.audience: The Jewish community in Jerusalem after exile.
Nehemiah.purpose: To recount the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and the community's renewed commitment to covenant life.
Nehemiah.theme: God's work includes both rebuilding a city and reforming a covenant community.
Nehemiah.summary: Nehemiah leads a rapid rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls despite opposition, then joins Ezra in public Scripture reading and covenant renewal before addressing ongoing social and religious problems.

movements.title: Walls Rebuilt
movements.description: Nehemiah organizes the people to rebuild Jerusalem's walls despite threats and opposition.

movements.title: Scripture Read and Covenant Renewed
movements.description: Ezra reads the law publicly, leading to confession, worship, and covenant commitment.

movements.title: Community Reforms
movements.description: Nehemiah addresses Sabbath observance, temple support, exploitation, and intermarriage concerns.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.description: Cupbearer to the Persian king, who becomes governor and leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.

keyFigures.name: Artaxerxes
keyFigures.description: The Persian king who grants Nehemiah permission and resources to rebuild.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.description: The priest and scribe who reads the law publicly to the people.

keyFigures.name: Sanballat
keyFigures.description: A regional official who leads opposition to the rebuilding.

keyFigures.name: Tobiah
keyFigures.description: An Ammonite official who opposes Nehemiah and is later expelled from a temple storeroom.

keyFigures.name: Geshem the Arab
keyFigures.description: Joins Sanballat and Tobiah in mocking and opposing the work.

keyFigures.name: Eliashib
keyFigures.description: The high priest, who helps rebuild the wall but later gives Tobiah a room in the temple.

Esther.author: Anonymous.
Esther.audience: Jews living in the Persian Empire and later Jewish communities commemorating Purim.
Esther.purpose: To explain the deliverance of the Jewish people from a planned massacre and the origin of the feast of Purim.
Esther.theme: Providence can preserve God's people even when God is not explicitly named.
Esther.summary: Esther, a Jewish woman who becomes queen, risks her life to expose Haman's plot against the Jews. The threatened destruction is reversed, and Purim commemorates the deliverance.

movements.title: Esther Becomes Queen
movements.description: Esther becomes queen of Persia while concealing her Jewish identity.

movements.title: Haman's Plot
movements.description: Haman gains authority and secures a decree to destroy the Jews after conflict with Mordecai.

movements.title: Reversal and Deliverance
movements.description: Esther exposes Haman, the Jews are allowed to defend themselves, and Purim is established.

keyFigures.name: Esther
keyFigures.description: A Jewish orphan, also named Hadassah, who becomes queen and risks her life to save her people.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.description: Esther's cousin and guardian, whose refusal to bow to Haman triggers the conflict.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.description: The Persian king, commonly identified with Xerxes I, who chooses Esther as queen.

keyFigures.name: Haman
keyFigures.description: An Agagite official who plots to destroy the Jews and is executed on his own gallows.

keyFigures.name: Vashti
keyFigures.description: The queen deposed for refusing the king's summons, opening the way for Esther.
